This seems rather wasteful to allocate new arrays over and over just to use as arguments.

Wouldn't `TextDecoder.decode` automatically make sure we use the fastest possible implementation?

Good call — switched to a module-level `TextDecoder('latin1')` singleton in 489ba74. Uses the engine's native implementation, eliminates both the chunk-loop allocations and the explicit subarray calls.

I went with `'latin1'` (Windows-1252 in WHATWG encoding spec) rather than the default UTF-8 to keep the mapping bijective — UTF-8 would produce replacement characters (U+FFFD) for byte sequences that aren't valid UTF-8, which could cause distinct binary values to compare equal. Windows-1252 maps every byte value 0–255 to a unique code point, so the comparable-string guarantee holds for taint tracking.

We should make search asynchronous.

When the search input is updated, we should update it synchronously, e.g. just calling `setSearchTextState(text)`. But finding matches should be done in a transition, because otherwise it may block the update that will change the input text.

Keep controlled input updates sync, and put other updates in a transition.

Done. The controlled input now updates synchronously (setSearchTextState(text)), and the match computation is deferred: searchResults is derived from useDeferredValue(searchText), so the tree walk runs at transition priority and never blocks the input update. I went with useDeferredValue rather than startTransition since searchResults is a derived value — it's the transition-priority tool for derived data, and it keeps results scoped to the current commit for free (the memo re-derives on commit change). Selecting the current match now reacts to the deferred results.

for very long arrays this will do quite a bit of memory work and much of it potentially repeated since the entire tail is continued into each new task. If we're already making affordances for this notion we might as well support rendering from an index to avoid memory churn

Have just pushed up [a commit that does this approach](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/36053/commits/071f0c7ac72ef4dbe1c0ba9e3b31130c13edff8c)

I didn't change the `createTask` signature for the extra properties (as this is the only place they're used), but I can do it that way if prefered.

Also let me know if you'd prefer a separate branch / PR for this instead
Is this collection load-bearing?

This is all very much "gc as often as possible to be absolutely sure". GC isn't a fully deterministic thing so I wouldn't try to over-fit the GC calls to match the scenario currently. Same questions could be asked about the number of GCs we run before we give up. 100 is making sure. 1 might be sufficient **now**.

While I was writing this I forwarded the question to Fable medium and it had the same conclusion (good clanker 😇) :
> So the honest description of the second loop is: the ticks are what matter (destroy hooks fire asynchronously after collection), and the gc() calls are belt-and-braces for intermediate promises the WeakRef doesn't track, in case they need another pass once their retainers died in an earlier cycle. On current Node/V8 that extra collection changes nothing in either direction, but it costs microseconds and guards against GC-behavior drift across Node versions, so I'd leave it.
try blocks prevent the containing function from being optimized. Can you find a way to solve this problem without adding a new try block? Maybe by fixing it in `unwindContext`?

I could move the call to `instance.render` into a separate function that is try/finally wrapped to minimize the impact. (I'm not an expert with the whole inlining area.) In its currently form I think it would be difficult to fix things in `unwindContext`.

Although I'm working today on an effort to combine `ReactFiberContext` and `ReactFiberHostContext` and add fiber-level tracking so that we won't pop a Fiber more than once, or pop one that wasn't pushed. It will hopefully ease the pressure here a bit as it would enable us to just dev-warn and ignore the bad pop rather than throw an error.
I don't think this check is an optimization tbh. it's checked in `parseModelString` and will just return the value there.

The check is duplicated, but the point is avoiding the function call. `parseModelString` is a large function with many switch cases, so neither GCC nor V8 will inline it. Without the guard, every non-`$` string (class names, text content, attribute values, etc.) pays for argument setup, stack frame push/pop, the same `value[0] === '$'` check inside, and return. With the guard, those strings never enter the function. I haven't measured the impact though, so it would be good to verify with your benchmarks.

We should try to avoid recursion when not necessary. For example, a pattern we typically use is check if something is resolved first and then initialize and then check if something is initialized instead of a single switch.

In this case, there can also be a lot of listeners when there's a lot of references to the same thing so in theory you can actually stack overflow because of this recursion.

Instead, you should check if the status has changed to initialized or errored here and if so call `wakeChunk` or `rejectChunk` respectively.
We shouldn't create the closure outside the condition. Maybe it's optimized but we should make sure.
But it's used in both branches of the condition.
In that case you should move it out to a reusable function in module scope and then call that from the closure. So that the closure only needs to be allocated in the delayed branch.
Then `addDebugInfo` can be hoisted out.
